title: AWS Global Infrastructure
description: Learn how AWS organizes its global network of Regions, Availability Zones, and edge locations.

data.text: AWS operates a vast global network of data centers called Regions. Each Region is a physical location in the world containing multiple isolated data centers called Availability Zones. This design lets you run applications that are both highly available and resilient to failures.

data.title: Why Multiple Regions?
data.text: Choosing a Region close to your customers reduces latency. It also helps you comply with data residency laws that require certain data to stay within a specific country or region.

rows: A geographic area containing multiple AZs. Each Region is isolated from others.
Choose a Region close to your users for low latency.
One or more discrete data centers with independent power, cooling, and networking.
Deploy applications across multiple AZs for high availability.
A site that caches content close to end users for faster delivery.
Used by CloudFront and Route 53 to reduce latency.
A small data center placed very close to a large population or industrial center.
Run low-latency applications in major cities.

data.text: Each Region contains at least three Availability Zones. AZs are physically separated by meaningful distances but connected with low-latency, high-throughput fiber links. This means if one AZ loses power or internet connectivity, the others keep running.

terms.definition: A geographic area containing multiple Availability Zones. Examples include us-east-1 (N. Virginia) and eu-west-1 (Ireland).
An isolated location within a Region made up of one or more data centers with independent power and networking.
An AWS endpoint for caching content close to users, used by CloudFront and Route 53.
A small data center placed close to a population center to deliver single-digit millisecond latency.

data.title: Using Regions in Practice
data.content: When you launch an EC2 instance, you choose a Region. You can then choose a specific AZ within that Region. For maximum resilience, you would launch instances in at least two different AZs so a failure in one does not take down your application.
data.code:
# View all available Regions
aws ec2 describe-regions --query 'Regions[*].[RegionName]' --output table

# View Availability Zones in a Region
aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --region us-east-1

data.title: Best Practices for Global Infrastructure
items: Launch resources in at least two Availability Zones for high availability.
Use edge locations through CloudFront to speed up content delivery.
Select a Region that complies with your data residency requirements.
Use Local Zones when you need very low latency for specific applications like gaming or real-time video.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Regions are geographic areas containing multiple isolated Availability Zones
AZs provide fault isolation and high availability
Edge locations improve performance by caching content closer to users
Choosing the right Region affects latency, cost, and compliance
data.takeaway: Next, you will learn about the tools AWS provides to manage your cloud resources.
